cards.title_en: Byblos (Jbeil) Maritime Harbor & Cedar Trade
cards.explanation: Byblos illustrates how coastal geography shaped eastern Mediterranean exchange networks: cedar timber and resin moved south to Egypt while papyrus (from which the Greek word biblion derived) moved north through Phoenician ports.

cards.title_en: Myth of Isis, Osiris, and the Sacred Tree of Byblos
cards.explanation: Plutarch’s De Iside et Osiride (chs. 15–16) embeds Byblos into Egyptian-Hellenistic mythography. Historians read the sacred tree-pillar episode not as literal biography, but as symbolic memory of Byblos’s role supplying sacred timber to Egypt.

cards.title_en: Afqa Spring, Nahr Ibrahim, and the Seasonal Myth of Adonis
cards.explanation: The Nahr Ibrahim / Afqa landscape demonstrates how ancient sacred geography mapped seasonal ecological cycles—specifically ferruginous limestone sediment runoff and anemone blooms—onto Levantine-Hellenistic ritual narratives.

cards.title_en: Sarcophagus of King Ahiram & the 22-Letter Phoenician Abjad
cards.explanation: Epigraphic analysis of the Ahiram sarcophagus situates the Byblian 22-letter abjad within a broader Canaanite/Proto-Sinaitic continuum. While maritime trade spread this script to Greece and Aramaic chancelleries, scholars reject simplistic monocausal origin myths.

cards.title_en: Writing, Recipes, and Oral Memory as a Portable Archive in the Lebanese Diaspora
cards.explanation: Expatriate literature (e.g., Maalouf, Alameddine) frames letters, dialect idioms, and recipes as portable archives that bridge generational migration—explored in-game through privacy-safe curated oral-history exhibits.

cards.title_en: Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) & Abbasid Translation Tradition
cards.explanation: While Bayt al-Hikma symbolizes the Abbasid translation movement, historians distinguish the well-documented network of court-sponsored translators from later idealized accounts treating the palace library as a modern university.

cards.title_en: Scholars of Baghdad: Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Kindi, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, Thabit ibn Qurra & Banu Musa
cards.explanation: The collaboration among al-Khwarizmi, al-Kindi, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, Thabit ibn Qurra, and the Banu Musa illustrates how philological translation (collating Greek and Syriac manuscripts) directly fueled experimental mechanics and algebraic theory.

cards.title_en: Contested Chronicles: Weight-in-Gold Payments & 1258 River-of-Ink Accounts
cards.explanation: Source criticism distinguishes primary 9th-century evidence from 13th–15th century literary topoi (such as Ibn Abi Usaybi’a’s gold-weight anecdote or later river-of-ink accounts of 1258), teaching players how historians evaluate chroniclers’ claims.

cards.title_en: Al-Mutanabbi Street, Shabandar Café & the International Book Solidarity Archive
cards.explanation: Al-Mutanabbi Street and the Al-Mutanabbi Street Starts Here artist-book archive exemplify cultural resilience: preserving Iraq’s pluralistic intellectual heritage across Baghdad and the global diaspora after 2007.

cards.title_en: Cardamom Date Kleicha, Shanasheel Courtyards & Plural Diaspora Memory
cards.explanation: Material culture in the Iraqi diaspora links architectural conservation (shaded shanasheel microclimates) and culinary heritage (regional kleicha variations across plural Iraqi communities) to intergenerational memory.

cards.title_en: Egyptian Fanous Lanterns & Competing Fatimid/Coptic Origin Narratives
cards.explanation: Rather than treating the 972 CE al-Mu’izz procession anecdote as a singular origin fact, urban historians examine how Fatimid street-lighting ordinances, Coptic liturgical lamps, and artisanal tin-working converged into Cairo’s fanous tradition.

cards.title_en: Cairo Lantern Metalwork, Stained Glass & Khayamiya Tentmaker Appliqué
cards.explanation: In Historic Cairo (UNESCO #89), the spatial proximity of Taht al-Rab’ lantern workshops and the Qasaba of Radwan Bey khayamiya guild sustains shared geometric design grammars across metal, glass, and textile media.

cards.title_en: Neighborhood Soundscapes: The Musaharati Drummer & Festive Cairo Chants
cards.explanation: Ethnomusicological study of Cairo’s Ramadan traditions highlights how acoustic community markers (the musaharati’s baz drum and oral refrains with contested Arabic/Coptic etymologies) map neighborhood social cohesion.

cards.title_en: Teta Samira’s Koshari & Inclusive Courtyard Hospitality
cards.explanation: Koshari’s evolution in modern urban Cairo reflects global trade circuits (combining Indian-inspired rice-and-lentil khichdi roots with Italian pasta and Egyptian garlic-vinegar daqqa) into a democratized national dish.

cards.title_en: Egyptian Diaspora Celebrations & Ontario Egyptian Heritage Month Candidate Fact
cards.explanation: Contemporary diaspora civic recognition—such as the source-cited Ontario Egyptian Heritage Month Act (2019, pending statutory verification)—illustrates how expatriate communities institutionalize cultural memory.

cards.title_en: The Traboules of Vieux Lyon and La Croix-Rousse
cards.explanation: Lyon’s traboules (UNESCO #872) exemplify high-density urban morphology. While tourism literature cites ~400–500 passages, urban historians distinguish verified public rights-of-way from private residential courtyards.

cards.title_en: The Canuts of La Croix-Rousse & Jacquard Punch-Card Silk Weaving
cards.explanation: The Jacquard loom (1804) transformed Lyon’s domestic silk industry (la Fabrique) by encoding warp-thread lifts on punched cards, reshaping both architectural typologies in La Croix-Rousse and the history of programmable machinery.

cards.title_en: Cour des Voraces, Labor Mutualism & Historical Memory in Lyon
cards.explanation: Historical analysis of the Cour des Voraces separates popular conflations (noting its c. 1840 construction postdates the 1831/1834 insurrections while anchoring the 1848 Voraces movement) and treats 1940s Resistance passage routes as non-trivialized civic heritage.

cards.title_en: The Mères Lyonnaises & Eugénie Brazier: Women-Led Culinary Craft
cards.explanation: The trajectory of the Mères Lyonnaises—culminating in Eugénie Brazier’s 1921 establishment and 1933 critical acclaim—demonstrates how working-class women chefs transformed regional bouchon traditions into modern gastronomic institutions.

cards.title_en: Galette des Rois, Kitchen Brigade Teamwork & Transnational Pastry Exchange
cards.explanation: Designing a community recipe archive requires documenting ingredient provenance, nut-free/gluten-aware substitutions, and non-edible fève safety notes while honoring cross-cultural culinary heritage.

cards.title_en: Bibimbap (Goldongban) & Regional Variants: Jeonju, Jinju, Tongyeong & Andong
cards.explanation: Textual attestation in late-Joseon cookbooks (Siuijeonseo’s goldongban) and regional specialization across Jeonju, Jinju, Tongyeong, and Andong demonstrate how a shared mixed-rice grammar adapts to local ecology and modern food-safety/allergen standards.

cards.title_en: Competing Origin Narratives of Bibimbap: Ritual, Court, Agriculture & Lunar New Year
cards.explanation: Historiographical analysis of bibimbap rejects single-origin essentialism: Eumbok ritual sharing,农번기 (nongbeongi) agrarian field meals, courtly goldongban, and seotdal geumeum household practices likely converged into modern regional forms.

cards.title_en: Obangsaek (오방색): Five-Color Cultural Symbolism & Harmony of the Bowl
cards.explanation: Obangsaek reflects East Asian cosmological aesthetics applied to Korean textile, architectural (dancheong), and culinary arts—understood by historians as a symbolic cultural framework for visual and nutritional variety rather than empirical science.

cards.title_en: Jeonju Hanok Village, Giwa Roofs, Nambu Market & Pungnammun Gate
cards.explanation: Jeonju Hanok Village illustrates urban heritage stewardship: maintaining over 700 timber-and-giwa structures alongside active civic spaces (Nambu Market, Pungnammun Gate) requires balancing tourism with resident privacy.

cards.title_en: Shared Bowls, Chuseok Songpyeon & Korean Diaspora Cultural Continuity
cards.explanation: Contemporary diaspora literature frames Korean foodways—from sourcing namul ingredients in expatriate grocery aisles to steaming Chuseok songpyeon—as living practices of cultural continuity and adaptation.
